card: Ten of Hawthorn · Ten of Wands
notes: Tone-under-load card. The three-kinds-of-stick taxonomy (assigned / assumed / simply nearest) might be the keeper here; everything else is scaffolding around it.

readingLine: Ten branches in one armload, and the gate still a field away. The load is real — no reframe on offer. But somewhere in the bundle are two sticks that were simply nearest when you bent down, and they weigh the same as the assigned ones.

Carrying everything at once as a way of not deciding what matters — the card catches you mid-haul, chin over the top stick. Nobody handed you all ten. Some were picked up on the way past, back when the pile was lighter.
question: Which stick in the load did nobody actually hand you?
What could go down first, and what truly breaks if it does?
libraryEntry: Ten of anything is a suit at maximum, and Hawthorn maxes out in armloads. The figure this plate implies — pips stacked nearly solid — is mid-carry: everything gathered, nothing delegated, the horizon reduced to the next hundred steps. It's the deck's most sympathetic card about competence, because the load is usually real and usually well-carried, and that's exactly how it grows. Reliable carriers get handed sticks. Then they start picking up unattended ones, since bending down is faster than negotiating. The card doesn't argue the season's demands away; harvests are heavy, and some of your weeks are tens. It only inventories. An armload that size holds three kinds of stick — assigned, assumed, and simply nearest — and at full stagger they're indistinguishable by feel. Sorting them mid-carry is not possible. It happens at the gate, sticks down, one at a time, which is the only part of the image the engraver left deliberately out of frame.

Hawthorn is the suit of work wanted and work chosen, which makes its ten a specific kind of heavy: the good life, all of it, at once. Nothing in the armload is junk. That's the trap. A load of obvious rubbish gets dropped without ceremony; a load where every stick is defensible gets carried until the carrier is the only indefensible part. The card tends to find people in their most respectable overwhelm — the calendar of things that all matter, the standing commitments that were each, individually, a yes worth giving. Ten doesn't ask which of them is worthless. Wrong question; no answers. It asks which of them is yours, which is subtler: duties drift, and a stick picked up in one season can ride along for three more on momentum and good posture alone. The bundle, notably, blocks the view forward. That isn't a metaphor the deck invented — it's just what carrying does, and why the gate matters more than the pace.
altText: Ten budded branch marks stacked in dense columns, nearly filling the plate's center.
A crowded plate: ten hawthorn sprig marks in close rows, ochre stamp above.
reversedReadingLine: The armload, set down — or dropped, which also counts. Reversed, the ten's weight is past tense and the shoulders haven't heard yet. Habits of bracing outlive their loads by seasons. You may be carrying the shape of the bundle, empty.

Reversed, the sticks scatter: something in the great carry has quit — a commitment lapsed, a duty handed back, maybe not gracefully. Relief and guilt arrive in you together, sharing a coat. Your field, worth noticing, is still standing, entirely unburnt.
reversedQuestion: What are you still braced for that already got put down?
Which dropped duty turned out to land without a sound?
reversedLibraryEntry: Reversed, the ten unbundles — sometimes by decision, more often by physics. A commitment finally lapses, a role gets handed back, a week simply refuses to close its fist around everything again, and you stand in the strange after-hush, lighter and slightly ashamed of it. The shame deserves examining, because it's usually borrowed. Somewhere the idea took hold that the full armload was the baseline self, and anything less a deficit. The card disagrees with the arithmetic. Ten was always the suit's ceiling, not its resting state; no other Hawthorn card carries more than it can see over. What follows a real setting-down is telling. A dropped stick that stays on the ground unmissed was momentum cargo, and the guilt is a habit clearing its throat. Something that genuinely wobbles can be picked back up — the hands are free now, which was rather the point. Either way, the shoulders take longest to believe it.

There's a harder reversal: the load kept upright past the body's vote. Reversed tens sometimes mark the carry that has stopped being work and become identity — the person, some seasons you, who cannot put the bundle down because, without it, it's unclear what would be left standing in the field. Every offer of help reads as an audit. Every lightened week lands as demotion. The hawthorn in the image blooms, and that detail earns its keep: this suit flowers under load, but nothing flowers under load indefinitely, and the card reversed is usually the stem talking. None of this calls for dramatic renunciation, which would just be the same intensity pointed backward. It tends to start smaller: one stick, handed to someone who offered, accepted with both hands in view. The revelation isn't the lighter bundle. It's the discovery — mildly insulting, then freeing — of how competently the handed-over stick gets carried by somebody else.
